method: houseFire.scale: deaths from accidental exposure to smoke, fire and flames (ICD-10 X00-X09, plus half of Y26, fires of undetermined intent) in the WHO Mortality Database, pooled over 2017-2024 (whatever years each country reported), age-standardised to the 2022 US population in three groups (0-14, 15-64, 65+) with World Bank population, and divided by the same rate for the United States (9.6 deaths per million crude, 9.75 age-standardised). Where CTIF World Fire Statistics No. 31 gives the country's 2020-2024 fire deaths per 100,000, that ratio to the US (1.07), corrected by the same age factor, is averaged with the death-registration ratio (geometric mean). Wildfire disasters inside the pooled years (Greece 2018, Portugal 2017, Australia 2019-20) are removed. Where the place-of-occurrence digit shows a smaller share of fire deaths at home than in the US (about 0.82), the ratio is scaled down (Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Turkey, Korea). Finally, because the model's US figure (10 micromorts) is for a home with no working smoke alarm, each ratio is multiplied by (1 - 0.84 x 0.55) / (1 - p x 0.55), where p is the country's share of homes with a working alarm (mostly guessed) and 0.55 the alarm's effect, so that the figure describes an alarm-less home in every country. Countries with no death registration (China, India, Indonesia, Nigeria) use GBD 2021 regional rates for fire, heat and hot substances against High-income North America, cut to the structure-fire share, and national fire statistics as a floor; Norway uses CTIF alone. coIncident.scale: accidental poisoning by gases (X47, plus half of Y17, undetermined intent), age-standardised the same way, relative to the US, then multiplied by 1.42: 1.3 because only about 65% of US X47 deaths are carbon monoxide (624 accidental CO deaths in 2022 against 960 X47 deaths) against about 85% elsewhere, 1.5 because only about 40% of US CO deaths occur at home (fire-co.json) against about 60% elsewhere, and 0.73 because 49% of US homes have a working CO alarm and almost none elsewhere, so the observed rate understates the US alarm-less rate more. Small countries are shrunk toward a regional mean. China, India and Indonesia use GBD 2021 CO death rates against High-income North America (0.314 per 100,000).

reproduced.basis: By construction: the US death-registration rate (X00-X09 + half Y26, 3,195 deaths a year in 2017-2023, 9.6 per million) is the denominator for every country. NFPA home fire deaths (2,600-2,920 a year) are 85-90% of it. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

anchors.comment: Same as the preset. The ratio method assumes the US share of fire deaths that occur in homes (about 0.82-0.9) holds elsewhere unless the place digit says otherwise.

reproduced.basis: Population-weighted over the 18 Western European countries in this file: 0.41 before the smoke-alarm adjustment, 0.36 after it. United Kingdom alone: 0.39 before, 0.42 after (England's dwelling-fire deaths 3.6 per million against NFPA's 8.2 gave the preset 0.44). https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

anchors.comment: Preset 0.5 (0.3-1.0). The preset rounded England's 0.44 up and took no account of age (Europe is older, which raises crude rates) or of low alarm ownership in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece. My figure is inside the preset's range, at its lower end.

reproduced.basis: Argentina 2017-2023: X00-X09 216 a year plus Y26 (undetermined) 277 a year, counted at half; age-standardised ratio to the US 0.91. Times the alarm factor 0.57 (about 10% of homes with a working alarm, a guess) gives 0.52. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

anchors.comment: Preset 1.0 (0.4-2.0) was a guess with no national count. The registration data before the alarm adjustment, 0.91, confirm it. The alarm adjustment halves it, because the preset's figure applies to a home with no alarm, and nearly all Argentine homes are in that state already. Counting all of Y26 as accidental would give 1.25 before adjustment, none of it 0.57. The data are national, not for the city.

reproduced.basis: By construction: US X47 + half Y17, 1,004 deaths a year in 2017-2023 (3.0 per million), is the denominator. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

anchors.comment: Same as the preset. GBD 2021 gives High-income North America 0.314 per 100,000 age-standardised, consistent with X47, not with CDC's narrower count of about 1.6-1.9 per million.

reproduced.basis: Population-weighted X47 + half Y17 ratio over 18 Western European countries is 0.34; times 1.42 for the differences in gas mix, place and CO alarms gives 0.49, and the per-country shrinkage and the UK's factor (1.8) bring the weighted mean of the final figures to 0.51. GBD 2021: Western Europe 0.086 against High-income North America 0.314 per 100,000 (0.27 before the 1.42). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10602911/

anchors.comment: Preset 0.8 (0.3-1.3). The preset set French (1.5-2.0 per million, 2008) and German figures against CDC's narrower US count (1.6); registration data on a like-for-like code give Western Europe about a third of the US rate, and the 1.42 brings it back to about a half. Inside the preset's range, below its middle.

coIncident.scale.basis: X47 111 a year and Y17 95 a year counted at half; ratio 1.29, times 1.42. GBD Southern Latin America agrees. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

countries.notes: Fire before the alarm adjustment: 0.91. Argentina codes more fire deaths as undetermined than as accidental, so the treatment of Y26 is the largest uncertainty.

countries.name: Brazil

houseFire.scale.basis: WHO 2017-2023 ratio 0.60 (1,054 deaths a year); times 0.84 (69% of place-coded deaths at home); alarm factor 0.55 (5%, guess). https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

coIncident.scale.basis: X47 + half Y17 ratio 0.07, times 1.42; GBD Tropical Latin America 0.029 per 100,000 against 0.314 agrees. Warm climate, little indoor heating. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10602911/

countries.notes: Fire before the alarm adjustment: 0.50.

countries.name: China

houseFire.scale.basis: No registration data. GBD 2021 East Asia, fire, heat and hot substances, 0.6 against High-income North America 0.65 per 100,000 (0.92); times 0.77 for the larger share of scalds; times 0.6 for an urban home (rural houses and coal heating carry most deaths, a guess); alarm factor 0.57. Official counts (CTIF: 0.08 per 100,000) are a floor. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12091820/

coIncident.scale.basis: GBD 2021: China 0.8 per 100,000 age-standardised against High-income North America 0.314 (2.55); times 1.42; times 0.5 because coal heating in rural north China carries most deaths (guess). https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1642416/full

countries.notes: Both figures rest on GBD modelling of China's sample registration and on a guessed urban discount.

countries.name: India

houseFire.scale.basis: NCRB: 5,888 fire-accident deaths in 2024, about 60% residential, 2.4 per million against the US home 8.6 (0.28), times 2-4 for under-recording; GBD South Asia 1.9 per 100,000 against 0.65 (2.9) times a structure-fire share of 0.25 (0.73). Middle 0.7, times alarm factor 0.55. https://insights.dataful.in/articles/nearly-6000-fire-accident-deaths-in-2024-despite-sharp-decline-in-accidents

coIncident.scale.basis: GBD 2021 South Asia 0.068 per 100,000 against 0.314 (0.22), times 1.42 = 0.31; raised slightly for winter brazier (angithi) deaths in closed rooms in the north that GBD may miss. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10602911/

countries.notes: Most Indian burn deaths are cooking and clothing burns, not house fires, which smoke alarms do not address; they are left out.

countries.name: Indonesia

houseFire.scale.basis: GBD 2021 Southeast Asia 0.7 per 100,000 against 0.65 (1.08), times a guessed structure-fire share of 0.6/0.97, times alarm factor 0.55. Dense urban kampungs burn often. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12091820/

coIncident.scale.basis: GBD 2021 Southeast Asia 0.101 per 100,000 against 0.314 (0.32), times 1.42. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10602911/

countries.notes: Regional GBD figures only.

countries.name: Nigeria

houseFire.scale.basis: GBD 2021 Western sub-Saharan Africa 3.9 per 100,000 against 0.65 (6.0), times a guessed structure-fire share of 0.35 and alarm factor 0.55 = 1.15, lowered because GBD's figure there is modelled (UI 1.7-5.4) and urban housing is mostly masonry. CTIF's 0.07 per 100,000 is a fire-service fragment. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12091820/

coIncident.scale.basis: GBD 2021 Western sub-Saharan Africa gives only 0.15 of the US rate, but nightly generator use is widespread and press estimates run from 100 to about 1,400 generator deaths a year (0.5-6 per million, search snippets); at about 1.5 per million and a home share near 1, against the US 1.9 per million of CO deaths, about 1.2.

countries.notes: No death registration. The least certain country for both fields.

countries.name: Philippines

houseFire.scale.basis: WHO 2017-2019 ratio 0.62 (young population; crude 0.41) and CTIF (0.29 per 100,000) ratio 0.41, mean 0.50; alarm factor 0.55 (5%, guess). https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

coIncident.scale.basis: X47 ratio 0.08 and GBD Southeast Asia 0.32, geometric mean 0.16, times 1.42. Registration coverage is incomplete. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

countries.notes: Fire before the alarm adjustment: 0.50.

countries.name: South Africa

houseFire.scale.basis: WHO 2017-2020: X00-X09 2,519 deaths a year (41 per million), ratio 5.0; times 0.8 for non-structure burns (guess); alarm factor 0.55 = 2.2, lowered to 2.0 because informal-settlement shack fires weigh less in an average urban home. GBD Southern sub-Saharan Africa 5.1 against 0.65 per 100,000 agrees. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

coIncident.scale.basis: South Africa codes almost all gas deaths as undetermined (Y17 224 a year against X47 10): counting 80% of Y17 gives a ratio of 1.18, GBD Southern sub-Saharan Africa 0.57; middle 1.0, times 1.42. Braziers and paraffin heaters. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

countries.notes: Fire before the alarm adjustment: 4.0.

blockedSources: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/fire-death-rates.csv (and api.ourworldindata.org indicator 1165066): GBD 2023 age-standardised fire death rates for every country; 403, licence-restricted.
https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/: country-level GBD 2021 rates for fire and for carbon monoxide; interactive tool, not attempted.
https://factly.in/data-between-2014-2022-madhya-pradesh-maharashtra-and-gujarat-accounted-for-more-than-50-of-all-fire-accidents: NCRB residential fire deaths for India (403).
WHO Mortality Database documentation PDF: the age-format codes were applied from the file layout and known WHO conventions, not read from the document.
Norway: absent from the WHO ICD-10 files; national cause-of-death data (Statistics Norway) not fetched.
Bomberos de Chile and Argentine fire-service totals: not found, so Chile's and Argentina's registration counts could not be checked.
openQuestions: The smoke-alarm adjustment follows the definition (the US 10 micromorts is for a home without a working alarm), but it was not applied to the presets. On this method the buenosAires preset would be about 0.5, not 1, and westernEurope about 0.36, not 0.5. The figures before adjustment are in each country's notes if the owner prefers to drop it.

houseFire.scale also multiplies the property-loss dollars. It is calibrated on deaths only; property losses in US dollars should probably also scale with price level, which this family does not supply.
Alarm ownership by country is mostly guessed. It would be better as an 'already owned' default per country, since the model's smoke-alarm item is the main thing this scale feeds.
Latvia (3.1), Estonia (2.7), South Africa (2.0) and Lithuania (2.0) are two to three times the US: check that nothing in the engine assumes the scale is at most about 1.
The CO factor of 1.42 (gas mix, home share, CO-alarm ownership) is a guess common to every country but the US, the UK and Canada; it decides the level of every CO figure against the US.
Urban versus national: registration data are national; only China gets an explicit urban discount.
